Vignette:
Eighteen-year-old Leila had always been proud of her keen eye for detail, a trait that served her well in her architectural studies. But since witnessing a devastating car crash on her daily commute six months ago, Leila's sharp instincts had become a double-edged sword. As she lay in bed each night, she couldn't shake the feeling that she needed to stay alert, just in case something terrible happened again. She would find herself scanning her darkened room for potential threats, ears straining to pick up any unusual sounds. That fateful day still replayed vividly in Leila's mind: the screech of tires, the crunch of metal, and the anguished cries of the injured drivers. What haunted her most was the image of a young mother, her face smeared with blood, stumbling out of the wreckage. Leila had watched helplessly as bystanders rushed to assist, feeling an overwhelming sense of guilt for not being able to do more. As the weeks went by, Leila's fear and anxiety began to seep into every aspect of her life. She would become irrationally angry when a friend or family member was late responding to a text, convinced that something terrible must have happened to them. Her usual enthusiasm for design projects waned as she found herself constantly on edge, anticipating some unknown disaster. Leila's hypervigilance had also started to affect her daily routine. She would arrive at campus hours before classes began, feeling an intense need to survey the surroundings and ensure everything was "safe." Her friends had begun to notice a change in her behavior, commenting on how jumpy she seemed in crowded spaces or when sudden noises startled her. One particularly difficult day, Leila's anxiety boiled over during a studio session. As she worked on a project, the sound of a nearby classmate's laughter sent her heart racing, transporting her back to the scene of the accident. She hastily gathered her belongings and rushed out of the room, feeling ashamed and embarrassed by her reaction. Her avoidance behaviors had started to take a toll on Leila's relationships and academic performance. Her friends were growing increasingly concerned about her withdrawal from social activities, while her professors noted a decline in the quality of her work. The tension between Leila's creative passion and her newfound fear was suffocating her. As she sat in the therapist's office, Leila confessed that it was the realization of how much her life had changed – and not for the better – that finally prompted her to seek help. She feared losing herself entirely to this constant sense of threat, but a part of her held onto hope: perhaps with therapy, she could learn to trust her own resilience once more and rediscover the calm, creative person she used to be.
